lit.\u0027\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv class=\":
"
1 · Reactivity of the derivative
"
lit.\u0027\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp class=\":
"

Rule: substitution proceeds toward the derivative with the more basic leaving group (more stable). Chloride → anhydride → ester → amide.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cb\u003eAdición–eliminación\u: "Addition–elimination: tetrahedral intermediate and expulsion of L⁻."
lit.\u0027\u003cb\u003eSaponificación\u003c/: "Saponification is irreversible because of carboxylate formation; acid hydrolysis is an equilibrium."
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eCon \u003cb\u003eHO⁻\:
"

With HO⁻ the ester becomes carboxylate + alcohol. The last step, deprotonation of the acid by the alkoxide or HO⁻ (pKa 4.76 versus 15.9), is so favorable that it drives the whole equilibrium: irreversible saponification. In acidic medium, by contrast, hydrolysis is an equilibrium (the reverse of Fischer esterification).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl mejor grupo salien:
"

The best leaving group is the weakest base (lowest pKa of the conjugate acid HL): Cl⁻ (HCl, −7) > CH₃COO⁻ (4.76) > RO⁻ (≈ 16) > NH₂⁻ (38). That is why reactivity decreases: chloride > anhydride > ester ≳ acid > amide. A more reactive derivative is converted into a less reactive one, never the other way around (without activation).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl par libre de L se:
"

The lone pair of L is delocalized toward the C=O (resonance form L⁺=C–O⁻): N > O > Cl in donating ability. The more L donates, the lower the δ+ on C and the less reactive the derivative, and also the lower the C=O IR frequency (the C=O gains single-bond character): chloride ≈ 1800, anhydride 1820/1760, ester ≈ 1740, amide ≈ 1650 cm⁻¹. The blue spheres are the pairs of L; the orange ones, the δ+ of the carbonyl.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn la \u003cb\u003eam:
"

In the amide the N donates its pair to the C=O: the O=C–N group is planar and rotation about the C–N bond has a barrier of ≈ 70–90 kJ/mol (partial double-bond character). That is why amides are poorly electrophilic, hydrolyze only with strong acid or base and heat, and form the backbone of peptides (peptide bond).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa sustitución acílic:
"

Acyl substitution is a two-step addition–elimination: (1) the nucleophile attacks the C=O and forms the tetrahedral intermediate (O⁻); (2) the O⁻ pair regenerates the C=O and expels L⁻. Unlike attack on aldehydes and ketones, here the intermediate has a good leaving group. The barrier of the first step is lower the more electrophilic the carbonyl is.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos \u003cb\u003ederi:
"

Acid derivatives share the acyl group R–C(=O)– bonded to an L group (Cl, OCOR, OR′, NR′₂). They can be converted into the carboxylic acid by hydrolysis. What differentiates their reactivity is L: how much it donates its electron pair to the C=O (resonance) and how good a leaving group it is.

"
